messages.subject: Reporting on repeated rows
messages.body_plain:
---plyr 1.5.2 on R 2.13.0, Windows 7 64-bit---

I have a dataset with (intentionally) repeated rows and I want to report on the number of repetitions.

The following code works:

> row.counts <- function (r)
>     arrange(
>        ddply(r,
>              names(r),   # all columns
>              function(a) cbind(a[1,],count=nrow(a))),
>        desc(count))
>
> > test <- data.frame(a=c(1,2,3,1,2,3),b=c(1,2,1,2,2,1))
> > row.counts(test)
>   a b count
> 1 2 2     2
> 2 3 1     2
> 3 1 1     1
> 4 1 2     1

... but doesn't seem very elegant.

Next, I wanted the rows within each group with the same count to be ordered lexicographically.  The best I could come up with was

> row.counts.sort <- function (r) {
>     counted <-
>        ddply(r,
>              names(r),
>              function(a) cbind(a[1,],count=nrow(a)))
>     arrange(counted,desc(count),do.call(order,counted))
> }
>
Can someone do better?  ... or suggest extensions/changes to plyr which would handle these cases more elegantly?

             -s

messages.subject: Re: Reporting on repeated rows
messages.body_plain:
Yup, that's it!  Thanks for the quick and helpful reply!

But wouldn't it be more consistent with the plyr paradigm to have it called like this (a la subset and mutate)?:

> ddply( test, ...columns..., count )

The main problem there is specifying all columns.  Count lets you do that by omitting the column spec:

> count(test, ) == count(test, vars=NULL)

but ddply (reasonably enough) does not:

> > ddply(test,,function(r) cbind(r[1,],freq=nrow(r)))
> Error in as.quoted(.variables) :                                          <<<< no default
>   argument ".variables" is missing, with no default
>
And an explicit NULL variable spec means the opposite of what it does in count.  The ddply definition seems more consistent: .() = NULL means no grouping variables.  Perhaps TRUE can mean all grouping variables, something like Top <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_type>.
>
> > ddply(test,.variables=NULL,function(r) cbind(r[1,],freq=nrow(r)))
>    .id a b freq                                                                    <<<< NULL means NO variables, not ALL variables
> 1 <NA> 1 1    6
>
The signatures are inconsistent, too:

> args(ddply)

function (.data, .variables, .fun = NULL, ..., .progress = "none", .drop = TRUE, .parallel = FALSE)

> args(count)

function (df, vars = NULL, wt_var = NULL)

Why df vs. .data and vars vs. .variables?  .progress doesn't seem necessary for count, but .drop certainly makes sense.

           -s

messages.subject: Summarizing % of total and % of category ?
messages.subject_clean: Summarizing % of total and % of category ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to figure out how to create a summary of data that includes
a column for indicating the row's percentage of the total statistic
(i.e. all data) and of its parent category's total.

I've read "The split-apply-combine strategy for data analysis" but
still can't quite figure out how to do this efficiently.  I'm trying
to overcome the shortcoming of Excel's pivot tables, which do not
allow for calculating % of categories.

For example (using the 'baseball' data set) ... Given all data for
2007 where the number of home runs is greater than zero, summarize the
data using the following columns: League, Player ID, # of HRs, % of
Total HRs, % of League's Total HRs.

The following code creates the first three columns ... but not sure
where to go from there.

myfun <- function(x) sum(x$hr)
baseball <- subset(baseball, year == 2007 & hr > 0)
df2007 <- ddply(baseball, .(lg, id), myfun)
names(df2007)[3] <- "HR"

Might anyone have any recommendations?

Many thanks,
Mauricio

messages.subject: Re: Summarizing % of total and % of category ?
messages.subject_clean: Summarizing % of total and % of category ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here is a two stage approach: one for the league percentages and one
for the overall MLB percentages. The key in ddply() is that an
external function passed into it needs to take a data frame as input,
and output a scalar or data frame; in this case, you want the latter.

myfun <- function(df) {
    hrpct <- with(df, round(100 * hr/sum(hr), 3)
    data.frame(id = df$id, hr = df$hr, pctlg = hrpct)
   }

bb07 <- subset(baseball, year == 2007 & hr > 0)
bb07lg <- ddply(bb07, .(lg), myfun)   # returns percentages of league HRs
ddply(bb07lg, .(), transform, pctmlb = round(100 * hr/sum(hr), 3))[, -1]

The [, -1] part at the end of the last statement removes a column of
unnecessary NAs.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Inconsistency in .() grouping case of ddply
messages.subject_clean: Inconsistency in .() grouping case of ddply
messages.body_plain:
plyr 1.5.2 R 2.13.0

When grouping by .(), there is an extra .id column which is always NA (that is, adds no value).  If we are grouping by n columns, shouldn't exactly n grouping columns be included in the result?

> ddply(data.frame(a=1:2,b=1:4),.(),nrow)
   .id V1                                    ### 1 group column for 0 grouping vars
1 <NA>  4
> ddply(data.frame(a=1:2,b=1:4),.(a),nrow)
  a V1                                       ### 1 group column for 1 grouping var
1 1  2
2 2  2
> ddply(data.frame(a=1:2,b=1:4),.(a,b),nrow)
  a b V1                                     ### 2 group columns for 2 grouping vars
1 1 1  1
2 1 3  1
3 2 2  1
4 2 4  1

Also, the split_labels attribute is of an inconsistent class:

> class(attr(dlply(data.frame(a=1:2,b=1:4),.(),function(x)1),'split_labels'))
[1] "NULL"
> class(attr(dlply(data.frame(a=1:2,b=1:4),.(a),function(x)1),'split_labels'))
[1] "data.frame"

Shouldn't it be an empty data.frame?

The zero case is just as valid as the 1, 2, 3 cases....

           -s

messages.subject_clean: Summarizing % of total and % of category ?
messages.body_plain:
To my mind, the "natural" way to solve this is with nested ddply's, since the problem statement is also nested.

e.g.

ddply(baseball,
      .(),
      function(all) {
         total <- sum(all$hr)
ddply(all,
      .(lg),
      function(league) {
         lg_total <- sum(league$hr)
 ddply(league,
       .(id),
summarize,
HR=sum(hr),
HRlg=sum(hr)/lg_total,
HRtot=sum(hr)/total
)})})

Unfortunately, there is a bug in the handling of variable scope in ddply, so this won't work.  Instead, you have to use <<- (!):

ddply(baseball,
      .(),
      function(all) {
         total <<- sum(all$hr)
ddply(all,
      .(lg),
      function(league) {
         lg_total <<- sum(league$hr)
 ddply(league,
       .(id),
summarize,
HR=sum(hr),
HRlg=sum(hr)/lg_total,
HRtot=sum(hr)/total
)})})

A disadvantage of this approach is that you can't take advantage of the implicit scope rules of ddply, where a column name standing on its own refers to the column of the current data frame, thus you need to write, e.g. league$hr instead of hr.

There is another bug that introduces the meaningless .id column in the result....

           -s

messages.subject: mutate vs. summarize assignment semantics
messages.body_plain:
mutate has the handy feature that it performs its column assignments sequentially rather than in parallel (the document says "iteratively", which isn't quite right...)

> mutate(data.frame(a=(1:5)^2),q=median(a),r=a-q)
   a q  r
1  1 9 -8
2  4 9 -5
3  9 9  0
4 16 9  7
5 25 9 16

But summarize does not:

> summarize(data.frame(a=(1:5)^2),q=median(a),r=mean(a)-q)
Error in mean(a) - q : non-numeric argument to binary operator

Goose, gander, sauce?

          -s

messages.subject: Count and ddply and arrays
messages.body_plain:
> count(matrix(1:9,3,3))
  X1 X2 X3 freq
1  1  4  7    1
> count(matrix(rep(1,9),3,3))
  X1 X2 X3 freq
1  1  1  1    1

These don't seem like useful results. Count should either do something sensible or give an error for non-dataframes.

> count(floor(1:4/2))
  x freq
1 0    1
2 1    2
3 2    1

For a vector argument, count is actually useful -- but this case isn't mentioned in the documentation and isn't consistent with ddply's handling of vectors:

> ddply(floor(1:4/2),.(),print)
Error in rep(1, nrow(data)) : invalid 'times' argument

 And it is bizarre that count considers the elements of a vector to be in column "x":

> count(floor(1:4/2),"x")
  x freq
1 0    1
2 1    2
3 2    1

Actually, I think count should be done away with and replaced with a better way to refer to "all columns" in ddply.  More flexible and more orthogonal.

Similarly, ddply doesn't seem to check its argument type if it is an array:

> ddply(matrix(1:9,3,3,dimnames=list(c("a","b","c"),c("d","e","f"))),"d",sum)
Error in FUN(X[[1L]], ...) : numeric 'envir' arg not of length one

It might be sensible to convert it to data.frame (though there must be a more efficient way of grouping array rows by value?):

> ddply(as.data.frame(matrix(1:9,3,3,dimnames=list(c("a","b","c"),c("d","e","f")))),"d",sum)
  d V1
1 1 12
2 2 15
3 3 18

messages.body_plain:
This is actually a really challenging problem to solve because of the
mix of dynamic and lexical scoping.  One work around is to explicitly
define a function:

local({
  a <- 2
  df <- data.frame(q = 1:3)
  ddply(df, "q", function(piece) {
    mutate(piece, r = q / a)
  })
})

I have tried to fix it properly once only to fail.  lapply works
around the problem by manually constructing and evaluating calls at
the C-level, which I'd really rather avoid.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: two matrix and correlation
messages.body_plain:
Here are some ways to do it:

> > m1 <- matrix(runif(20),4,5)
> > m2 <- m1 + rnorm(20)/10
>
Map over the row index:

> > laply(1:nrow(m1),function(i) cor(m1[i,],m2[i,]))
> [1] 0.9890534 0.8604399 0.9242942 0.9884833

Of course, that is no different from core R's sapply in this case:
>
> > sapply(1:nrow(m1),function(i) cor(m1[i,],m2[i,]))
> [1] 0.9890534 0.8604399 0.9242942 0.9884833
>
Map cor over the lists of rows (plyr doesn't have anything corresponding to mapply):

> > mapply(cor,alply(m1,1),alply(m2,1))
>         1         2         3         4
> 0.9890534 0.8604399 0.9242942 0.9884833
>
This last approach seems the cleanest in the absence of a multi-array version of aaply (e.g. syntax could be aaply(list(m1,m2),1,cor) or maaply(cor,1,m1,m2) ), but it is much less efficient.

I'd have thought that mlply could solve this, but the best I could do with mlply was the very long and ugly:

> as.numeric(mlply(data.frame(a=I(alply(m1,1)),b=I(alply(m2,1))),function(a,b) cor(a[[1]],b[[1]])))

Take advantage of the matrix case of cor:

> adply(array(c(m1,m2),c(dim(m1),2)),1,cor)

This looks the most R-like in style to me (and there's probably a better way to build an n+1 -dimension array from two n-dimension ones)....

I'd have expected it to be as fast as the sapply approach, but in fact it is almost as slow as the mapply/alply approach.

               -s

messages.subject: Re: Variable scope bug in ddply
messages.body_plain:
I think it's an important problem to solve.  Otherwise you can't nest ddply in a natural way, as in

ddply(baseball,
      .(),
      function(all) {
         total <- sum(all$hr)     ## only works if changed to <<-
 ddply(all,
       .(lg),
       function(league) {
          lg_total <- sum(league$hr)  ## only works if changed to <<-
  ddply(league,
        .(id),
summarize,
HR=sum(hr),
HRlg=sum(hr)/lg_total,
HRtot=sum(hr)/total
)})})

Of course, if you change to <<-, not only is that ugly (and pollutes the global name space), but it presumably prevents you from using .parallel.

I don't see why it's a dynamic vs. static scope issue.  I'd have though it's a matter of constructing the correct environments and evaluating each thing in the right one.  But then, I'm not quite ready to volunteer to fix this myself....

          -s

> Hadley

>> >    local({a<-2; ddply(data.frame(q=1:3),.(q),mutate,r=q/a)})
>> >    Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'a' not found

ddply() hands down its "..." arguments to alply() and in turn to
llply(). By the time llply() is working, there's no way to tell which
environment the expression "q/a" was defined in.

It's an abstraction breakdown that R suffers when you want to pass
your arguments down to a worker function and that worker function does
nonstandard eval.

I think it could be fixed if there was a way to read off the
environment associated with a promise object. delayedAssign() lets you
construct promises with arbitrary expressions and environments, and
substitute() lets you read off the expressions, so to my mind there's
no reason not to be able to read off the environment.

(I might be characterizing the problem wrong. It's something I only
recently started banging my head against.)

Peter

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Jun 13, 2011 at 14:49, Peter Meilstrup <peter.m...@gmail.com> wrote:
> ddply() hands down its "..." arguments to alply() and in turn to
> llply(). By the time llply() is working, there's no way to tell which
> environment the expression "q/a" was defined in.
>
> It's an abstraction breakdown that R suffers when you want to pass
> your arguments down to a worker function and that worker function does
> nonstandard eval.

Well, clearly the topmost function needs to capture its enclosing environment and pass it to inner functions whenever expressions (as opposed to closures) are being passed around.

Naively, that doesn't seem that hard -- you just have an optional argument of every function which takes an expression as an argument which is the environment; and it defaults to environment().  The signature of ddply would be

function (.data, .variables, .fun = NULL, ..., .progress = "none",
    .drop = TRUE, .parallel = FALSE, .env = environment() )

and when it calls ldply it overrides the default, passing .env = .env.  And since .fun may perform non-standard evaluation, it needs a .env argument as well.

Problem: what if .fun *doesn't* have a .env argument?  It would be pretty ugly to have to do something like

        if (".env" %in% names(as.list(args(apply)))) ...

As I said above, "naively, that doesn't seem that hard".  I fiddled quickly with the code and couldn't make it work, but I'm afraid I need to get back to my regularly-scheduled job now....

           -s

> ddply() hands down its "..." arguments to alply() and in turn to
> llply(). By the time llply() is working, there's no way to tell which
> environment the expression "q/a" was defined in.

Well it is possible, but it's tricky - you need to capture the
parent.frame() (not the parent environment) when llply is called, and
then pass that down along the call stack.  I've managed to do that.

The challenge is then figuring out how to evaluate the function in the
right context so that it can access the variables in the environment
in which it was called (dynamic scope) as well as the variables
representing the data that's being process (lexical scope).  I could
never figure this out.

Hadley
